title: The Cursed Maiden
author: William Saville
content:
The wind rushed past her as she jumped, the cliffs jagged and sharp, she dove past them all, into the icy depths below. As she sank below the water, her only thoughts were that she wished for peace. Unfortunately, there is no peace for the undead. She rose back to the surface, and opened her mouth and let out a wail of despair. She need not fill her lungs with air to let out such a bellow, as her lungs had long ago decayed. More of her had fallen from the bones from her jump, but she felt nothing but emotional pain, as too, her nerves had long decayed. She swam out into the bitter seas, long stretches of nothingness. She would find her end out here, or at least, would no longer be compelled to hurt innocent people. She blinked nearly hollow eyes, and went onwards towards her hoped oblivion.

The curse clung to her bones as stubbornly as rot to flesh, an ancient hex uttered by a witch whose name time itself had forgotten. Long ago, the maiden had made a plea for vengeance; to punish a lover who betrayed her. The witch had granted her wish, but the price was steep: her humanity, her soul, her very mortality. She had been remade into a harbinger of sorrow, a weapon to destroy, but never to rest. The betrayal was avenged long ago, but the curse persisted, feeding on her despair and binding her to a ceaseless, empty existence.

When she finally emerged from the water’s surface after swimming many leagues below the dark waves of the sea, her wail carried over the waves, a sound so inhuman that the seagulls scattered like ash in a tempest. Her throat, ragged and decayed, had no need for air, but her anguish was a force of its own, defying nature. More flesh sloughed from her frame, her fingers reduced to sinew and bone, yet she felt nothing. No pain, no cold; only the weight of the curse gnawed at her mind, whispering its demands: Hurt. Destroy. Spread the sorrow.

She swam through the bitter sea, the salt stinging what remained of her skin but unable to reach the nerves that had rotted long ago. Days and nights blurred together, the horizon always the same desolate line. But the ocean held secrets even darker than her own.

It began with whispers; soft, guttural echoes rising from the depths. They seemed to call her name, though she hadn’t heard it spoken in centuries. At first, she thought it was the curse toying with her. But then, she saw them: faces half-formed, their eyes hollow voids, peering up from beneath the waves. These were not spirits; they were fragments of lives she had stolen, the innocents consumed by her compulsion to harm. Their forms drifted like kelp, reaching for her with skeletal hands.

“Leave me!” she cried, her voice reverberating like a broken bell. The faces only stared, their accusing silence more terrible than any scream. She turned away, but the sea seemed to close in around her, the water thickening like blood.

Days passed; or perhaps weeks. She found herself washed ashore on a jagged, blackened coast, the sand coarse as ground bone. The land was barren, save for a crooked forest of dead trees that stretched toward the storm-choked sky. The whispers followed her here, their voices growing louder, merging into a cacophony of lament.

Within the forest, she came across ruins; a crumbled chapel, its stones slick with moss and decay. Inside, a mirror hung from rusted chains, its surface warped and clouded. When she approached, it rippled, revealing not her reflection but a vision of what she had been: a young woman with eyes that held the light of stars. Her reflection reached out, mouthing words she couldn’t hear. The maiden tried to touch the glass, but her skeletal hand passed through, and the image shattered into a thousand screaming faces.

The curse spoke then, its voice seeping from the cracks in the walls, the whispers growing deafening: “There is no peace for you. There is only us. Only sorrow. Until there is nothing left.”

And so, she walked. Each step forward seemed to unravel her further. With every mile, her flesh abandoned her bones, piece by piece. First, her fingers; then, her arms; her ribs, her legs. Yet she moved onward, her body becoming a walking skeleton animated by the curse’s cruel will. The world itself seemed to bend under her presence, the sky growing darker, the air colder.

Eventually, there was nothing left to hold her together. Her last fragment of flesh; a sliver of her heart; crumbled to dust, and her bones collapsed into a heap on the barren ground. For a moment, there was silence.

But the curse did not allow oblivion.

The wind picked up, swirling the bones into the air. They knit themselves together once more, her hollow skull clattering into place. A faint light flickered where her heart had been, a cruel imitation of a soul. She stood, her form now entirely skeletal, a grim figure that exuded despair.

She wandered into the ruins, drawn to a flickering glow within the chapel. There, she found a book bound in human skin, its pages filled with runes that seemed to writhe when she looked at them. The whispers grew louder, hissing promises of freedom if she completed their ritual. But as her bony fingers traced the symbols, the faces of the innocents she had harmed appeared once more, etched into the walls around her.

Their silent pleas rooted her in place. Was this the end she sought, or was it just another layer of torment?

As she hesitated, the curse lashed out, screaming through her mind: “Choose! Oblivion or servitude!”

For the first time in centuries, the maiden made a choice. She dropped the book into the flickering light, watching as the flames consumed it. The curse shrieked in rage, the chapel quaking as though the earth itself was trying to swallow her whole.

When the smoke cleared, she was alone. The whispers were gone. Her bones, though still bare, felt lighter. She looked down at her skeletal hands, unsure if she was finally free or if the curse was merely silent, waiting.

The horizon called to her once more, but this time, it was not with despair; it was with the faintest glimmer of hope.
